title: Noise in Current Mirrors and Differential Pairs
intro: A current mirror copies the noise of its reference device along with its current, multiplied by the mirror ratio. A differential pair has two devices in the signal path, so its input noise power is twice that of a single CS stage.

blocks.text: Mirror $I_{REF}$ through $M_{REF}$ into M1 with $(W/L)_1 = N(W/L)_{REF}$, $N$ around 5 to 10 to save reference current. $M_{REF}$'s gate noise appears at its gate through its own $1/g_{m,REF}$, so a capacitor $C_B$ at the shared gate filters it. With $\overline{V_{n,REF}^2} = N\overline{V_{n1}^2}$ for flicker noise (area ratio $N$, equal lengths):

For the reference noise to be negligible, $(N - 1)g_{m,REF}^2 \ll C_B^2\omega^2$ at the lowest frequency of interest, which can demand nanofarads. Adding a resistor $R_B$ between the reference gate and $C_B$ lowers the filter corner to $1/[(1/g_{m,REF} + R_B)C_B]$, dividing the required $C_B$ by $1 + g_{m,REF}R_B$:

blocks.alt: Current mirror: IREF from VDD into diode-connected MREF; MREF's gate connects through resistor RB to the gate of M1, which has a capacitor CB to ground. M1's drain carries ID1.
blocks.caption: An RC filter between the reference and the output device.

blocks.text: $R_B$ can be large before its thermal noise rivals the reference device's flicker noise; the limit is area (and DC error from gate leakage through $R_B$). A long, narrow MOSFET biased at a small overdrive serves as a compact $R_B$. The noise of the reference current itself (often from a bandgap) also passes through.

With the inputs tied, the two device noise currents are uncorrelated, so node P is not a virtual ground for them. Still, half of $I_{n1}$ flows in each load and the two halves add (they are correlated) to $I_{n1}R_D$ differentially. With the loads' noise:

blocks.alt: Resistively loaded differential pair M1, M2 with tail current ISS; a noise voltage source Vn1 squared in series with M1's gate and Vn2 squared in series with M2's gate.
blocks.caption: Moving each device's noise to its gate gives the result directly.

blocks.text: That is twice the CS value (in power), since there are two devices in the signal path; for the same $g_m$ per device the pair also burns twice the current. A fully differential circuit's input noise power is twice that of its half circuit. With current-source loads M3 and M4:

The five-transistor OTA (mirror load) gives the same thermal result, $8kT\gamma(1/g_{m1,2} + g_{m3,4}/g_{m1,2}^2)$: the short-circuit output current is $4kT\gamma(2g_{m1,2} + 2g_{m3,4})$, since M3's noise circulates in the diode and is copied by M4. Again, make the load $g_m$ small relative to the input pair's.

In a balanced pair the tail noise splits equally and only moves the common mode. Off balance it slightly modulates $g_m$ ($g_m \approx g_{m0}(1 + I_n/2I_{SS})$), which is usually negligible. In the OTA, though, the output follows the mirror node, so tail noise appears at the output as $\overline{I_n^2}/(4g_{m3}^2)$ even with equal inputs.

A pair biased at tiny current can serve as a large floating resistor of about $2/g_{m1}$, but it is noisier than a real resistor of the same value (and nonlinear): the noise between its two outputs is $8kT\gamma(g_{m1} + g_{m3})/g_{m1}^2$ plus flicker terms.

blocks.title: Bypass capacitor for a mirror
blocks.text: A 1:4 mirror ($N = 4$) has $g_{m,REF} = 2\text{ mS}$. The lowest frequency of interest is 100 kHz, and the reference flicker noise should be suppressed tenfold, i.e. $C_B^2\omega^2 = 10(N - 1)g_{m,REF}^2$. Find $C_B$, then $C_B$ with $R_B = 50\text{ k}\Omega$.
blocks.answer: 17 nF without $R_B$; about 170 pF with $50\text{ k}\Omega$.

blocks.title: Pair against CS
blocks.text: Each device has $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$, $\gamma = 1$, and $R_D = 5\text{ k}\Omega$. Compare the input thermal noise of a CS stage and a differential pair.
solution: Pair: twice the power, $4.27\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ ($\sqrt{2}$ times larger).

blocks.title: OTA noise
blocks.text: A five-transistor OTA has $g_{m1,2} = 2\text{ mS}$, $g_{m3,4} = 1\text{ mS}$, $\gamma = 1$. Find the input thermal noise density.
solution: $\sqrt{2.48 \times 10^{-17}} = 4.98\text{ nV}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$; the load adds half as much as the pair.
